hook: The same answer can cost 10× more or arrive 5× slower depending on engineering. **Caching, routing, streaming, fallbacks** — the optimization stack, honestly prioritized.

scenes.title: Three caches, three wins: **prompt, response, semantic**
scenes.sub: The highest-ROI optimizations in the whole stack
scenes.narration: Caching is the first lever because it's pure win — same answers, less spend, less latency. PROMPT CACHING: many providers cache the PREFIX of your request — system prompt plus tool schemas, which are identical across calls; subsequent calls bill the cache read at a fraction of full price. Exploit it: put static content first, dynamic content LAST — reorder your prompt assembly so nothing variable appears early, or you bust the cache on every call. RESPONSE CACHING: exact-match cache — same question, same answer settings → serve the stored response; perfect for FAQ traffic, near-zero cost, and with GA-17's tenant-scoping rule for keys. SEMANTIC CACHING: the fuzzy version — embed the question, serve cached answers for near-duplicates above a similarity threshold — 'what's the refund policy' in twelve phrasings, one generation. Threshold discipline from GA-17: high — 0.95-plus — or wrong answers get served fast.

cards.s: Provider-side prefix reuse · static-first assembly · fractions of full price
Exact match → instant · FAQ goldmine · tenant-scoped keys
Near-duplicate questions → cached answer · high threshold · QA the hits

scenes.narration: Composition order matters: check response cache first — exact match is free and instant; then semantic — paraphrase coverage; then the live call, whose result gets stored in both. Cache INVALIDATION deserves a policy: prompt-version changes must version the cache keys, or old-prompt answers leak into new-prompt traffic; TTLs on semantic entries, because cached answers age — a 'refund policy' answer from six months ago is a liability. And measure what GA-24 promised: cache hit-rate and cost-per-request on one dashboard — a healthy system's hit-rate line tells you your traffic's repetitiveness, which in turn tells you how much MORE caching could buy. One caution: never cache ERROR paths or abstentions as successes — the cache key must include enough of the request's context that a 'not found' today doesn't become 'not found' forever.

scenes.title: Model routing: **cheap first, strong when needed**
scenes.sub: Not every question deserves your best model
scenes.narration: The insight: question difficulty varies wildly, but teams historically pay top-model prices for ALL of it. Routing sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it: a classifier — or cascade — triages: simple FAQ → small model; complex reasoning → flagship. The cascade pattern: try the cheap model with a confidence check; if its self-assessed confidence — or a verifier pass — falls short, escalate to the stronger model. Savings of fifty to eighty percent are routine, because MOST traffic is easy. The failure mode to engineer: misrouted hard questions getting cheap-model answers with confident delivery — so the escalation check must be EXTERNAL — verified, not self-reported — and quality monitoring from GA-24 slices per route, proving the cheap lane isn't quietly degrading. Model routing composes with prompt caching — smaller models, shorter prompts, cached prefixes — the savings multiply.

layers.s: Classifier or rules: length, topic, sensitivity → route
Small/fast model · prompt cache · full guardrails
External check: verifier pass or golden-sample score · below bar → flagship lane
Flagship model · only the traffic that earns it

scenes.narration: Three design decisions define a routing system. WHO triages: a fine-grained classifier, an LLM self-rating, or simple rules — start with rules — 'questions under twenty words about pricing → cheap lane' — and graduate to learned triage only when the logs show rules misrouting. WHAT verifies: the escalation check can be a second cheap model grading the first, a retrieval check — 'did the cheap answer cite the same chunks as the strong lane would?' — or periodic golden-lane sampling — score the cheap lane against known answers and watch the delta. And WHICH questions never route cheap: anything safety-adjacent, anything with side effects, anything the compliance contract names — some traffic pays full price BY POLICY. Route the rest; the invoice shrinks without the quality bar moving.

scenes.title: Latency: streaming, parallelism, **and smaller contexts**
scenes.narration: Users judge responsiveness by TIME TO FIRST TOKEN — half a second of streaming beats five seconds of buffered waiting, even when total time is identical. Streaming is table stakes — PY-12's SSE consumption, PY-13's SSE emission — the loop from LLM to browser stays open. Parallelism: independent calls run together — retrieval and guardrail prechecks, multiple tool calls — asyncio.gather, PY-10; serialize only true dependencies. Smaller contexts: latency scales with context length — trim system prompts, cap retrieved chunks, AG-13's budget discipline pays in milliseconds too. And batch where the user isn't waiting: overnight embedding jobs, background summarization — cheap models, batch APIs, off-peak rates. The composite: a request streams its first token fast, fans out its independent work in parallel, and carries the smallest context that answers — that system FEELS instant even when the total compute is unchanged.

items.s: LLM → server → browser, all SSE (PY-12/13) · first token in <1s
gather() for independent calls · only true dependencies serialize
Latency scales with tokens · trimmed prompts, capped retrieval, budget discipline

scenes.narration: RESILIENCE belongs in the same chapter because latency without fallback is fragility. Multi-provider fallback: the pipeline holds a primary provider and a secondary; on 429s or 5xxs beyond retry budgets — PY-12's tenacity — traffic fails over, possibly to a degraded mode — 'answers may be slower, we're on backup capacity'. Response SHAPE stays constant across providers — the exit contract your users depend on regardless of who's answering today. Idempotent retries complete the picture: a retried request must not double-charge or double-send — AG-02's idempotency rule at the infrastructure layer, client-request IDs deduplicating replays. A system that degrades gracefully — slower, cheaper, still correct — outlasts any system that's fast until the day it isn't.

scenes.title: Quotas & throughput: **capacity is a design input**
scenes.sub: PTU vs pay-as-you-go, rate limits, and planning
scenes.narration: Providers sell capacity two ways: pay-as-you-go — per-token pricing with rate limits — and provisioned throughput — PTU — reserved capacity at fixed cost, predictable latency, enterprise-grade. The decision math: PTU wins when utilization is HIGH and steady — your baseline traffic — reserved capacity costs less than equivalent on-demand and removes rate-limit surprises; pay-as-you-go wins for spiky, uncertain, or growing workloads — you pay for what you use and scale without commitments. Most mature systems blend: PTU for the baseline, on-demand for the peaks. Engineering around rate limits: client-side token buckets — smooth your own traffic rather than hitting provider walls — with queue-and-degrade patterns: when limits tighten, non-urgent work queues, urgent work passes, and the product degrades by FEATURE, not by crashing. And plan capacity from observability: GA-24's dashboards give the utilization curves that make the PTU-versus-on-demand math honest.

cards.s: Spiky/growing traffic · zero commitment · rate limits bite at peaks · cost = usage
High steady baseline · predictable latency/cost · reserved capacity · commitment risk
PTU the baseline, on-demand the peaks · client token buckets · queue-and-degrade under pressure

scenes.narration: The queue-and-degrade pattern deserves the last word: under capacity pressure, the system sheds load INTELLIGENTLY — background jobs pause, heavy features throttle, core answers keep flowing — the difference between a slow afternoon and an outage report. Design the degradation ladder in advance — which features pause first, second, third — because deciding during an incident means deciding badly. And rehearse: load-test against your own limits quarterly — rate limits, PTU ceilings, cache behavior under pressure — capacity surprises are self-inflicted when the dashboards existed to predict them. This reel's stack — caches, routing, streaming, fallbacks, quotas — compounds: each lever multiplies the others, and together they turn a workable system into an efficient one. Stage 8 closes with deployment: putting it all in an environment that promotes safely.

scenes.title: Fast and cheap, observed and controlled. Now ship it safely.

recap: Three caches compound: static-first prompts for provider cache reuse, exact response cache, high-threshold semantic cache — with versioned keys and TTLs
Model routing sends easy traffic to cheap lanes with EXTERNAL verification and policy exceptions; PTU covers the steady baseline, on-demand the peaks
Latency = streaming + parallelism + small contexts; resilience = multi-provider fallback with constant response shapes and idempotent retries; capacity pressure sheds load by design

quiz.q: Why must prompt caching dictate prompt ASSEMBLY order?
opts: Provider prefix caches only the static beginning — variable content placed early busts the cache on every call
quiz.why: The cache is positional: static system prompts and schemas first, dynamic user content last — assembly order is a billing decision.

quiz.q: Why must routing's escalation check be EXTERNAL rather than the cheap model's self-assessment?
opts: A model that answers wrongly usually believes it's right — external verification (verifier pass, golden sampling) catches what self-report can't
quiz.why: Confidence is not correctness: the failure mode — confident wrong answers in the cheap lane — requires an independent check to detect.

quiz.q: When does provisioned throughput (PTU) beat pay-as-you-go?
opts: High, steady baseline utilization — reserved capacity costs less than equivalent on-demand and removes rate-limit surprises; spiky traffic stays on-demand
quiz.why: PTU is a capacity commitment — it pays off exactly where demand is predictable; blend: PTU the baseline, on-demand the peaks.

code.title: The request pipeline with every lever in place
code.body:
async def handle(q, user):
    key = cache_key(q, user.tenant, prompt_version())
    if hit := response_cache.get(key):            # exact
        return hit
    if near := semantic_cache.search(embed(q), 0.95):
        return near                               # paraphrase

    route = triage(q)                             # cheap | strong
    try:
        async with token_bucket(user):            # smoothing
            stream = route.model.stream(assemble_static_first(q))
            return await emit_sse(stream,         # first token <1s
                                  on_complete=lambda r: (
                                      response_cache.set(key, r),
                                      semantic_cache.add(q, r)))
    except ProviderUnavailable:
        return await fallback_provider.handle(q)  # same shape, degraded note
annot: Cache reads precede everything; writes happen on completion — the pattern is read-shortcut, write-through
token_bucket smooths per-user traffic — client-side politeness beats provider rate-limit errors
fallback keeps the response CONTRACT constant — users see 'slower today', never a different shape

notes:
# Performance & Cost

## Caching
- Prompt cache: static-first assembly (positional).
- Response cache: exact match, tenant-scoped keys.
- Semantic cache: high threshold (≥0.95), TTLs, versioned keys, never cache errors/abstentions.

## Model routing
- Cheap lane first, EXTERNAL verification, escalate on miss.
- Policy exceptions: safety/side-effects/compliance stay flagship.
- Quality monitored per route (GA-24).

## Latency & resilience
- Streaming everywhere · gather() independent calls · smallest sufficient context.
- Multi-provider fallback, constant response shapes, idempotent retries.

## Quotas & throughput
- PTU for steady baselines, on-demand for peaks; token buckets; queue-and-degrade ladder designed in advance; load-test quarterly.
